purpose: Joke of the day for the Yoga Mom Talk and OhioMom front pages, and who is in the picture that day. Only jokes with approved true are published; the owner approves each batch before it runs. cast lists the children drawn that day, by first name (the first one answers the joke; an empty list is Deborah alone); pose and sweater are optional. Whatever a joke leaves out takes its turn.

jokes.text: I headed out to yoga and said “namaste.” My toddler said, “No, mama stay.” She won.
My favorite yoga pose is child’s pose. My child’s favorite is climbing on my back while I do it.
Mom coffee comes in three temperatures: hot, cold, and found in the microwave at bedtime.
Why are moms so good at balance poses? Years of carrying a kid, a bag and a conversation at the same time.
Bedtime is at 8. Requests for water, one more story and the meaning of life begin at 8:01.
Downward dog was going great until the actual dog joined in.
Laundry is the only workout where the weights multiply while you rest.
My kid can’t hear “shoes on” from two feet away, but can hear a snack wrapper from the next county.
Yoga has warrior one, two and three. Moms have warrior four: “Who drew on the wall?”
I asked for five minutes of peace. I got it, in installments.
Motherhood is finding a rock in the washer and knowing exactly whose pocket it came from.
Savasana: lie still, eyes closed, do nothing. I have been practicing it at 6 a.m. for years. It’s called pretending to be asleep.
My toddler’s favorite food is whatever is on my plate.
Tree pose is easy. Try it with a kid hanging off each branch.
Deep breath in. Deep breath out. Repeat until the shoes are on.
Nothing in the world is quieter than a toddler who has just found the markers.
Meditation is sitting quietly and noticing your thoughts. All of mine are, “Did I switch the laundry?”
I finally found my inner peace. It was under the couch with the missing sock.
My yoga class said to bring a block. I brought forty. They were already in my bag, next to one tiny shoe and a banana.
I can’t remember why I walked into this room, but I know every word of a cartoon theme song from three years ago.
“Happy baby” is a real yoga pose. Keeping a baby happy at 3 a.m. is a much more advanced practice.
“Because I said so” is just mom for “trust the process.”
My stretching routine: reaching under the car seat for a snack that fell in 2022.
Mom math: to be somewhere by 9, start getting everyone ready at 7 and arrive at 9:20.
Mountain pose: stand tall and still. Also known as waiting for someone to find the other shoe.
I don’t need an alarm clock. I have a small person who announces the sunrise.
The floor is lava. The couch is a boat. I am, apparently, the snack bar.
Yoga taught me to see the light in everyone. Motherhood taught me to see the light in the hallway that somebody left on.
A toddler’s “I do it myself” adds eleven minutes and a lot of pride.
Every load of laundry goes in with twelve socks and comes out with eleven. I have stopped asking questions.
Delilah saw me in tree pose and did what any toddler does with a tree. She climbed it.
Ephraim is good at math. He worked out that my “five more minutes” lasts twenty-two, on average. He showed his work.
Genevieve only wears black now. Laundry has never been easier to sort. Finding one particular black shirt has never been harder.
Atlas is our hide-and-seek champion. His favorite spot is behind a plant that is smaller than he is. We check everywhere else first. It’s only polite.
I asked Delilah to use her inside voice. It turns out she has one voice, and it goes everywhere she goes.
I’m tall. Ephraim is gaining on me fast. These days I do mountain pose mostly to check who’s still taller.
Genevieve wears all black. I wear a lot of pink. Side by side we look like a flamingo and its very serious shadow.
Atlas doesn’t need words to say he loves me. He uses a running start.
Delilah’s favorite word is “no.” Her second favorite is “NO.” They mean different things, and I have learned which is which.
Ephraim is a teenager now. I’ve stopped asking what he wants for dinner. I ask how much.
I told Genevieve her outfit was cute. She was crushed. The look she was going for was “haunting.”
Atlas hides. Delilah points at him and announces where he is. Hide-and-seek at our house lasts about nine seconds.
Ephraim checked my grocery math in his head and found I was off by forty cents. I’ve decided to be proud instead of annoyed. Mostly.
Delilah already knows what she wants to be when she grows up: in charge.
Genevieve’s sigh has perfect yoga form: full breath in, slow release, nothing held back. It was about socks.
I closed my eyes to meditate. When I opened them, Atlas was two inches from my face, grinning. Best jump scare of my life.
With four kids, somebody is always hungry, somebody is hiding, somebody is sighing and somebody is saying no. I can take attendance with my eyes closed.
Ephraim and Genevieve finally agree on something: my jokes aren’t funny. I’m calling it family bonding.
Warrior two is my strong pose. Delilah’s strong pose is standing in a doorway with her hands on her hips. Hers works better.
Atlas is tall for his age, which means the top shelf is no longer the safe shelf. There is no safe shelf.
Genevieve says her style is not a phase. Good, because I just bought her a third pair of black boots.
I asked Ephraim to do the dishes. He pointed out that, mathematically, they’ll just get dirty again. He’s right. He’s also doing the dishes.
I gave Delilah two choices for breakfast. She picked a third one, which I had not offered and do not have.
Atlas gives hugs like it’s his job. If it paid by the hug, he could retire by kindergarten.
Delilah wants to dress just like her big sister. So now there’s a very small goth in my kitchen, demanding juice.
Ephraim counted my sweaters and asked whether there’s a maximum. There is not. Math can’t answer everything.
Genevieve drew our family in her anime style. I have never had bigger eyes or better hair. It’s staying on the fridge forever.
Delilah helped me roll up my yoga mat. It now has one shoe, a spoon and a sticker rolled up inside it. I decided not to look any further.
Ephraim outgrew his new shoes in the time it took me to find the receipt.
I can hold a pose for ten breaths. Atlas can hold a hiding spot for about two. Then he giggles and gives himself away. I hope he never gets better at it.
